exercises.title: All employee records
exercises.instructions: The HR team needs a complete view of the employee records. Return every column for every employee.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT * FROM employees;
hints: Use the wildcard when every column is required.
exercises.explanation: SELECT * returns all columns from the table, with one result row per employee.

exercises.title: Student contact list
exercises.instructions: Display each student’s first name, last name and email address, in that column order.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM students;
hints: List only the three requested columns.
exercises.explanation: The SELECT list controls both which columns appear and their displayed order.

exercises.title: Product catalogue names
exercises.instructions: The online catalogue needs product names and current unit prices. Display those two fields.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, unit_price FROM products;
hints: Choose the descriptive and numeric columns from products.
exercises.explanation: A basic SELECT can retrieve columns of different data types from one table.

exercises.title: Unique employee departments
exercises.instructions: List each department ID represented among employees once.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT DISTINCT department_id FROM employees;
hints: Use DISTINCT on the selected column.
exercises.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows; NULL, if present, is retained as one distinct value.

exercises.title: Different customer cities
exercises.instructions: Show the different cities in which customers are located, without duplicates.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers;
hints: The city column contains repeated values.
exercises.explanation: DISTINCT applies to the complete selected row and removes repeated city values.

exercises.title: Distinct course and subject combinations
exercises.instructions: List each unique combination of course subject area and credit value.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT DISTINCT subject_area, credits FROM courses;
hints: DISTINCT applies to both selected columns together.
exercises.explanation: The result contains distinct pairs, not separate unique lists for each column.

exercises.title: Consultant details with aliases
exercises.instructions: For a staffing sheet, show consultant first names as “given_name” and hourly rates as “rate”.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name AS given_name, hourly_rate AS rate FROM consultants;
hints: Use AS to assign temporary result-column names.
exercises.explanation: AS changes the displayed column label without changing the stored table column.

exercises.title: Employees in the IT department
exercises.instructions: Display the first and last names of employees whose department ID is 20.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name FROM employees WHERE department_id = 20;
hints: Filter the rows on department_id.
exercises.explanation: WHERE keeps only rows for which the equality condition is true.

exercises.title: High-value products
exercises.instructions: List product names and prices for products costing more than 500.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, unit_price FROM products WHERE unit_price > 500;
hints: Use a numeric greater-than comparison.
exercises.explanation: The comparison is applied to each product before rows are returned.

exercises.title: Students from Ghent
exercises.instructions: Display the first and last names of students living in Ghent.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name FROM students WHERE city = 'Ghent';
hints: Text values are written in single quotes.
exercises.explanation: Text equality comparisons are case-sensitive in the course examples.

exercises.title: Projects not yet completed
exercises.instructions: Show the project names whose status is not completed.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, project_status FROM projects WHERE project_status <> 'completed';
hints: Use the not-equal operator.
exercises.explanation: The <> operator excludes rows whose status is completed.

exercises.title: Customers registered before 2022
exercises.instructions: Show customer names and registration dates for customers who joined before 1 January 2022.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, joined_on FROM customers WHERE joined_on < '2022-01-01';
hints: Use a date comparison with a strict less-than operator.
exercises.explanation: The strict < operator excludes the boundary date itself.

exercises.title: Out-of-stock items
exercises.instructions: List the names and stock quantities of products with zero stock.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, stock_quantity FROM products WHERE stock_quantity = 0;
hints: Zero is a numeric value, not NULL.
exercises.explanation: Equality to zero finds products whose stored stock quantity is exactly zero.

exercises.title: Students with no scholarship balance
exercises.instructions: Show students whose scholarship amount is exactly zero. Do not include missing scholarship values.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, scholarship_amount FROM students WHERE scholarship_amount = 0;
hints: A comparison to zero does not match NULL values.
exercises.explanation: Zero is a known numeric value, whereas NULL represents missing or unknown information.

exercises.title: Orders in processing
exercises.instructions: Display order IDs, dates and statuses for orders that are currently marked processing.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT order_id, order_date, order_status FROM orders WHERE order_status = 'processing';
hints: Use a text equality condition.
exercises.explanation: WHERE returns only orders with the exact stored status text.

exercises.title: Sales employees above a salary threshold
exercises.instructions: Show the names and salaries of employees in department 10 who earn more than 50000.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE department_id = 10 AND salary > 50000;
hints: Both conditions must be true for a row to remain.
exercises.explanation: AND combines the department and salary tests, so both restrictions apply.

exercises.title: Customers in selected cities
exercises.instructions: Display customer IDs and names for customers located in either Antwerp or Brussels.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Antwerp' OR city = 'Brussels';
hints: At least one of the city conditions must be true.
exercises.explanation: OR includes a row that matches either city value.

exercises.title: Open projects with a medium budget
exercises.instructions: List names and budgets for projects that are active and have budgets between 60000 and 180000.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, budget FROM projects WHERE project_status = 'active' AND budget BETWEEN 60000 AND 180000;
hints: Combine a status test with an inclusive numeric range.
exercises.explanation: AND requires the project to be active and the budget to fall inside the inclusive range.

exercises.title: Exclude completed and cancelled orders
exercises.instructions: Display orders whose status is neither completed nor cancelled.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT order_id, order_status FROM orders WHERE NOT order_status IN ('delivered', 'cancelled');
hints: NOT reverses the membership condition.
exercises.explanation: NOT applied to IN excludes all rows whose status appears in the specified list.

exercises.title: Students meeting either criterion
exercises.instructions: Show students who live in Antwerp or have a scholarship amount greater than 1000.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT student_id, first_name, last_name, city, scholarship_amount FROM students WHERE city = 'Antwerp' OR scholarship_amount > 1000;
hints: Use OR because either condition is sufficient.
exercises.explanation: The row is included when at least one of the two conditions is true.

exercises.title: Consultants with two specialty constraints
exercises.instructions: List consultants in Data or Cloud whose hourly rate is at least 100.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, specialty, hourly_rate FROM consultants WHERE (specialty = 'Data' OR specialty = 'Cloud') AND hourly_rate >= 100;
hints: Parentheses keep the OR alternatives together before applying the rate test.
exercises.explanation: The parentheses ensure the minimum rate applies to both specialties.

exercises.title: Employees outside selected departments
exercises.instructions: Return employees with a known department ID that is neither 10 nor 20.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, department_id FROM employees WHERE NOT department_id IN (10, 20);
hints: Use NOT with IN to exclude multiple department IDs.
exercises.explanation: NOT IN keeps rows whose department ID does not match either listed value; NULL department IDs are not included.

exercises.title: Orders within a quarter
exercises.instructions: Display order IDs and dates for orders placed from 1 April through 30 June 2025, including both endpoints.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2025-04-01' AND '2025-06-30';
hints: BETWEEN includes both boundary values.
exercises.explanation: The inclusive BETWEEN range keeps dates equal to either endpoint as well as dates between them.

exercises.title: Students with mid-range scholarship
exercises.instructions: Show student names and scholarship amounts from 400 through 1200 inclusive.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, scholarship_amount FROM students WHERE scholarship_amount BETWEEN 400 AND 1200;
hints: The lower value must come before the upper value.
exercises.explanation: BETWEEN includes both 400 and 1200; NULL values do not satisfy the range.

exercises.title: Products in selected categories
exercises.instructions: List product names and category IDs for products in categories 1, 3 or 5.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, category_id FROM products WHERE category_id IN (1, 3, 5);
hints: IN is a compact alternative to several equality tests.
exercises.explanation: IN matches any one of the listed category IDs.

exercises.title: Projects with active or paused status
exercises.instructions: Return projects whose status is active or paused and whose budget is below 150000.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, project_status, budget FROM projects WHERE project_status IN ('active', 'paused') AND budget < 150000;
hints: Use IN for status alternatives and AND for the budget limit.
exercises.explanation: The IN condition accepts either status; the separate AND condition limits the budget.

exercises.title: Employees within a salary band
exercises.instructions: Display employee names and salaries for salaries between 50000 and 70000 inclusive.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 70000;
hints: Use an inclusive range condition.
exercises.explanation: BETWEEN includes salaries exactly equal to either boundary.

exercises.title: Customer city and credit filter
exercises.instructions: List customers from Ghent or Leuven who have a credit limit above 1500.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, city, credit_limit FROM customers WHERE city IN ('Ghent', 'Leuven') AND credit_limit > 1500;
hints: Combine an IN test with a numeric comparison.
exercises.explanation: The AND requires a matching city and a credit limit above the threshold.

exercises.title: Employees hired after 2020 outside Operations
exercises.instructions: Show employee names and hire dates for employees hired after 31 December 2020 who are not in department 40.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, hire_date, department_id FROM employees WHERE hire_date > '2020-12-31' AND NOT department_id = 40;
hints: Combine a date comparison and a negated equality.
exercises.explanation: The query first requires a later hire date and then excludes department 40.

exercises.title: Names beginning with M
exercises.instructions: Find student first and last names where the first name begins with M.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name FROM students WHERE first_name LIKE 'M%';
hints: The percent wildcard stands for any number of following characters.
exercises.explanation: The pattern M% matches values beginning with M, including a one-character value.

exercises.title: Products ending in Adapter
exercises.instructions: Find product names that end with the word Adapter.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name FROM products WHERE product_name LIKE '%Adapter';
hints: Place the percent wildcard before the ending text.
exercises.explanation: %Adapter matches any prefix followed by the exact suffix Adapter.

exercises.title: Descriptions containing wireless
exercises.instructions: Display product names and descriptions containing the sequence wireless.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, description FROM products WHERE description LIKE '%wireless%';
hints: Use a percent wildcard at both ends to search within text.
exercises.explanation: The pattern matches rows with wireless anywhere in the description; matching is case-sensitive.

exercises.title: Four-character category codes
exercises.instructions: List category names and codes whose code contains exactly four characters.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT category_name, category_code FROM categories WHERE category_code LIKE '____';
hints: Each underscore represents exactly one character.
exercises.explanation: Four underscores match exactly four characters.

exercises.title: Employee email domains
exercises.instructions: Show employee names and email addresses for addresses ending in example.com.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM employees WHERE email LIKE '%@example.com';
hints: Use a pattern for the domain suffix.
exercises.explanation: The pattern finds the specified domain; employees with NULL email values do not match.

exercises.title: Consultant surnames with an internal sequence
exercises.instructions: Find consultant names whose surname contains the letters ore in that exact case.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name FROM consultants WHERE last_name LIKE '%ore%';
hints: Both wildcard characters allow text before and after the sequence.
exercises.explanation: The pattern matches the lowercase sequence ore at any position.

exercises.title: Employees without a department
exercises.instructions: List employees whose department assignment is missing.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name FROM employees WHERE department_id IS NULL;
hints: Use IS NULL rather than equality to NULL.
exercises.explanation: IS NULL tests for a missing department reference.

exercises.title: Customers with a known credit limit
exercises.instructions: Display customer names and credit limits only where a credit limit has been recorded.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, credit_limit FROM customers WHERE credit_limit IS NOT NULL;
hints: Use IS NOT NULL to require a stored value.
exercises.explanation: IS NOT NULL removes customers whose credit limit is missing.

exercises.title: Students missing email addresses
exercises.instructions: Return the IDs and names of students whose email address is unknown.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT student_id, first_name, last_name FROM students WHERE email IS NULL;
hints: A missing value must be checked with IS NULL.
exercises.explanation: NULL represents an absent or unknown value, not an empty string.

exercises.title: Orders without a shipping city
exercises.instructions: Find orders for which the shipping city has not been supplied.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders WHERE shipping_city IS NULL;
hints: Test the column with IS NULL.
exercises.explanation: The query returns orders whose shipping_city is unknown.

exercises.title: Project names with a fixed prefix
exercises.instructions: Display project IDs and names for projects whose name begins with Mobile or Research.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_id, project_name FROM projects WHERE project_name LIKE 'Mobile%' OR project_name LIKE 'Research%';
hints: Use two LIKE conditions joined with OR.
exercises.explanation: Either prefix is sufficient, so the patterns are joined with OR.

exercises.title: Filter missing and low credit limits
exercises.instructions: List customers whose credit limit is missing or whose known credit limit is below 1000, but only for customers in Antwerp or Ghent.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, city, credit_limit FROM customers WHERE city IN ('Antwerp', 'Ghent') AND (credit_limit IS NULL OR credit_limit < 1000);
hints: Group the two credit conditions in parentheses before combining with city.
exercises.explanation: The parentheses make the missing-or-low-credit rule apply only after the city condition is satisfied.

exercises.title: Highest-paid employees first
exercises.instructions: Display employee names and salaries ordered from highest salary to lowest.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC;
hints: Use descending order for the largest value first.
exercises.explanation: ORDER BY salary DESC sorts from the highest salary to the lowest.

exercises.title: Alphabetical customer list
exercises.instructions: Show customer names and cities, sorted alphabetically by last name.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, city FROM customers ORDER BY last_name;
hints: Ascending order is the default.
exercises.explanation: ORDER BY last_name sorts alphabetically in ascending order by default.

exercises.title: Department then salary
exercises.instructions: Display employee names, department IDs and salaries; sort by department ID ascending and salary descending within each department.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, department_id, salary FROM employees ORDER BY department_id ASC, salary DESC;
hints: Each sort key can have its own direction.
exercises.explanation: Rows are grouped by department in ascending order, then salaries are descending within each department.

exercises.title: Product stock with price tie-breaker
exercises.instructions: List product names, stock quantities and prices, ordered by stock from lowest to highest, then price from highest to lowest.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, stock_quantity, unit_price FROM products ORDER BY stock_quantity ASC, unit_price DESC;
hints: Use two ORDER BY expressions with separate directions.
exercises.explanation: The second key is used only when stock quantities are equal.

exercises.title: Sort by an alias
exercises.instructions: Display project names and budgets under the alias planned_budget, sorted by that alias in descending order.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, budget AS planned_budget FROM projects ORDER BY planned_budget DESC;
hints: An output alias can be used in ORDER BY.
exercises.explanation: The alias planned_budget refers to the selected budget expression.

exercises.title: Missing consultant emails last
exercises.instructions: Show consultant IDs, names and email addresses, placing missing emails after all recorded addresses.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT consultant_id, first_name, last_name, email FROM consultants ORDER BY email ASC NULLS LAST;
hints: PostgreSQL supports explicit NULLS LAST sorting.
exercises.explanation: NULLS LAST puts rows with missing email values after non-NULL values in the ascending sort.

exercises.title: Birth date with missing values first
exercises.instructions: Display employee names and birth dates, with missing birth dates before known dates and known dates from oldest to newest.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, birth_date FROM employees ORDER BY birth_date ASC NULLS FIRST;
hints: Choose ascending date order and explicitly position NULLs.
exercises.explanation: NULLS FIRST places missing birth dates at the beginning while the remaining dates ascend.

exercises.title: Sort by selected position
exercises.instructions: Display product name, price and stock quantity, sorting first by price descending and then by the third selected column ascending.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, unit_price, stock_quantity FROM products ORDER BY 2 DESC, 3 ASC;
hints: ORDER BY can refer to the position of a selected column.
exercises.explanation: Position 2 means unit_price and position 3 means stock_quantity in the SELECT list.

exercises.title: Second page of projects
exercises.instructions: The project list is sorted by project ID. Return rows 6 through 10 of that list.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_id, project_name FROM projects ORDER BY project_id OFFSET 5 FETCH NEXT 5 ROWS ONLY;
hints: Use a stable order, then skip five and fetch the next five.
exercises.explanation: The sorted result is paginated by skipping the first five rows and returning the next five.

exercises.title: First four students by birth date
exercises.instructions: Show the four students with the earliest birth dates.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT student_id, first_name, last_name, birth_date FROM students ORDER BY birth_date ASC FETCH FIRST 4 ROWS ONLY;
hints: Order from earliest date first, then limit the output.
exercises.explanation: The first four rows after ascending birth-date sorting are returned.

exercises.title: Next six employees by hire date
exercises.instructions: Display employee IDs, names and hire dates for employees 6 through 11 when ordered from newest hire to oldest.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, hire_date FROM employees ORDER BY hire_date DESC OFFSET 5 FETCH NEXT 6 ROWS ONLY;
hints: Skip five ordered rows before fetching six.
exercises.explanation: The query first sorts newest hires first, then returns positions 6 through 11.

exercises.title: Paged products within one category
exercises.instructions: For category 2, list the product names and stock quantities ordered alphabetically, skipping the first two and returning the next three.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, stock_quantity FROM products WHERE category_id = 2 ORDER BY product_name OFFSET 2 FETCH NEXT 3 ROWS ONLY;
hints: Filter, sort, and then apply pagination.
exercises.explanation: WHERE defines the category subset; ORDER BY establishes the page order, then OFFSET and FETCH select the requested page.

exercises.title: Employee directory for selected conditions
exercises.instructions: Show employees in departments 10, 20 or 30 whose salary is above 60000, sorted by department and surname.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, department_id, salary FROM employees WHERE department_id IN (10, 20, 30) AND salary > 60000 ORDER BY department_id, last_name;
hints: Combine IN and a salary comparison, then sort by two keys.
exercises.explanation: IN chooses eligible departments, AND applies the salary threshold, and ORDER BY organizes the resulting rows.

exercises.title: SKU pattern with one fixed character
exercises.instructions: Find products whose SKU has two characters, a hyphen, and exactly four further characters.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, sku FROM products WHERE sku LIKE '__-____';
hints: Underscore represents one character each time.
exercises.explanation: The pattern requires two characters, a hyphen, and four further characters.

exercises.title: Project completion date availability
exercises.instructions: Show project names and statuses for projects with no recorded end date, ordered by their start dates.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, project_status, start_date FROM projects WHERE end_date IS NULL ORDER BY start_date ASC;
hints: Filter missing dates with IS NULL before sorting.
exercises.explanation: IS NULL finds uncompleted-date records, and ORDER BY arranges them chronologically.

exercises.title: Retail orders in multiple statuses and dates
exercises.instructions: Display order IDs and dates for delivered or shipped orders placed during May or June 2025.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT order_id, order_date, order_status FROM orders WHERE order_status IN ('delivered', 'shipped') AND order_date BETWEEN '2025-05-01' AND '2025-06-30' ORDER BY order_date;
hints: Use IN for the status alternatives and BETWEEN for the inclusive date range.
exercises.explanation: The two conditions restrict the status and order date, then the result is sorted by date.

exercises.title: Rank customers by credit with NULLs last
exercises.instructions: List customer names and credit limits, with the largest known limit first and missing limits at the end.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, credit_limit FROM customers ORDER BY credit_limit DESC NULLS LAST;
hints: DESC reverses numeric order; NULLS LAST controls missing values.
exercises.explanation: The descending sort ranks high credit limits first and explicitly places NULL values last.

exercises.title: Top three consultant rates after excluding low rates
exercises.instructions: Return the second, third and fourth highest consultant hourly rates, with consultant names.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, hourly_rate FROM consultants WHERE hourly_rate >= 90 ORDER BY hourly_rate DESC OFFSET 1 FETCH NEXT 3 ROWS ONLY;
hints: Apply the minimum-rate filter before sorting and pagination.
exercises.explanation: WHERE removes rates below 90; descending order ranks the rest, and OFFSET/FETCH returns positions two through four.

exercises.title: What DISTINCT removes
exercises.instructions: What does DISTINCT do when used in a SELECT query?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: Limits the number of returned rows
exercises.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows; it does not sort or filter by NULL status.

exercises.title: Purpose of WHERE
exercises.instructions: At what stage does WHERE filter records?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before later grouping or sorting is applied.

exercises.title: Meaning of percent wildcard
exercises.instructions: In a LIKE pattern, what does % represent?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: Any amount of characters, including none
exercises.explanation: % matches any amount of characters, including zero characters.

exercises.title: Correct NULL test
exercises.instructions: Which condition correctly finds rows where email is missing?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.explanation: NULL must be tested with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL, not equality operators.

exercises.title: Default ORDER BY direction
exercises.instructions: What is the default sort direction when ASC or DESC is omitted?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.explanation: Ascending order is the default when the direction is omitted.

exercises.title: Purpose of OFFSET
exercises.instructions: What does OFFSET 10 do in a query result?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: Sorts the result by the tenth column
Filters rows whose values equal ten
exercises.explanation: OFFSET skips the specified number of rows in the ordered result.

exercises.title: Uppercase employee surnames
exercises.instructions: Create one employee display row containing the surname in uppercase, the first name in lowercase, and the original surname length.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT UPPER(last_name) AS surname_upper, LOWER(first_name) AS first_name_lower, LENGTH(last_name) AS surname_length FROM employees;
exercises.hints: Combine separate text transformations with a character-count result.
exercises.explanation: UPPER and LOWER standardize the two name fields independently, while LENGTH returns the character count of the surname.

exercises.title: Lowercase customer cities
exercises.instructions: For each customer, display the city in lowercase, the customer ID as a five-character code padded with leading zeroes, and the length of the original city.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT LOWER(city) AS city_lower, LPAD(CAST(customer_id AS VARCHAR), 5, '0') AS customer_code, LENGTH(city) AS city_length FROM customers;
exercises.hints: The numeric identifier must first become text before it can be padded.
exercises.explanation: LOWER standardizes the city, CAST makes the integer suitable for LPAD, and LENGTH measures the city text.

exercises.title: Formatted student names
exercises.instructions: Display each student name in title case as one full-name value, together with the email address in lowercase.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT CONCAT(INITCAP(first_name), ' ', INITCAP(last_name)) AS full_name, LOWER(email) AS email_lower FROM students;
exercises.hints: Format each name component before combining them.
exercises.explanation: INITCAP formats both name parts, CONCAT joins them with a space, and LOWER standardizes the email text.

exercises.title: Employee surname lengths
exercises.instructions: Display each surname in uppercase and its character count as a two-character text value padded with a leading zero when needed.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT UPPER(last_name) AS surname_upper, LPAD(CAST(LENGTH(last_name) AS VARCHAR), 2, '0') AS length_code FROM employees;
exercises.hints: Convert the numeric length to text before applying left padding.
exercises.explanation: LENGTH counts characters, CAST changes that count to text, LPAD formats the text width, and UPPER transforms the surname.

exercises.title: Product SKU prefixes
exercises.instructions: For every product, display a normalized SKU with the part before the hyphen in uppercase and the part after the hyphen in lowercase, joined by a hyphen.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT sku, CONCAT(UPPER(LEFT(sku, POSITION('-' IN sku) - 1)), '-', LOWER(SUBSTR(sku, POSITION('-' IN sku) + 1, LENGTH(sku)))) AS normalized_sku FROM products;
exercises.hints: Use POSITION to locate the separator, then extract the text on each side before combining the transformed parts.
exercises.explanation: POSITION finds the hyphen; LEFT extracts the prefix, SUBSTR extracts the suffix, UPPER and LOWER standardize case, and CONCAT joins the pieces.

exercises.title: Student email usernames
exercises.instructions: Display each student email and the username before the @ sign in lowercase, together with the number of characters in that username.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT email, LOWER(SUBSTR(email, 1, POSITION('@' IN email) - 1)) AS username, LENGTH(SUBSTR(email, 1, POSITION('@' IN email) - 1)) AS username_length FROM students WHERE email IS NOT NULL;
exercises.hints: Find the @ position and use it to determine the substring length.
exercises.explanation: POSITION identifies the separator, SUBSTR extracts the username, LOWER standardizes it, and LENGTH counts the extracted characters.

exercises.title: Find the dash in product SKUs
exercises.instructions: Show each SKU, its prefix before the hyphen, and its suffix after the hyphen. Return the prefix in uppercase and the suffix in lowercase.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT sku, UPPER(LEFT(sku, POSITION('-' IN sku) - 1)) AS sku_prefix, LOWER(SUBSTR(sku, POSITION('-' IN sku) + 1, LENGTH(sku))) AS sku_suffix FROM products;
exercises.hints: Use the separator position to calculate the start and length of each part.
exercises.explanation: POSITION locates the hyphen; LEFT and SUBSTR extract the two parts, and UPPER and LOWER standardize their case.

exercises.title: Standardize consultant specialties
exercises.instructions: Display each specialty in uppercase, replace any spaces with hyphens, and pad the result on the left to 16 characters using dots.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT specialty, LPAD(REPLACE(UPPER(specialty), ' ', '-'), 16, '.') AS specialty_code FROM consultants;
exercises.hints: Apply the case and replacement transformations before padding the final text.
exercises.explanation: UPPER standardizes the specialty, REPLACE changes spaces to hyphens, and LPAD adds leading dots to reach the requested width.

exercises.title: Clean customer names
exercises.instructions: Return each customer’s full name as one value, removing leading and trailing spaces from both name parts and capitalizing each word.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT CONCAT(INITCAP(TRIM(first_name)), ' ', INITCAP(TRIM(last_name))) AS clean_full_name FROM customers;
exercises.hints: Trim each part before applying title-style capitalization and concatenating them.
exercises.explanation: TRIM cleans both name parts, INITCAP capitalizes the words, and CONCAT joins the cleaned values with one space.

exercises.title: Remove leading z characters
exercises.instructions: Show employee street values after removing all leading lowercase z characters.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT LTRIM(LOWER(street), 'z') AS normalized_street FROM employees;
hints: First standardize case, then remove the specified leading character.
exercises.explanation: LOWER makes uppercase and lowercase letters consistent; LTRIM then removes leading z characters.

exercises.title: Build a consultant display name
exercises.instructions: Combine each consultant’s first and last name with one space between them.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) AS full_name FROM consultants;
hints: CONCAT combines values into one text value.
exercises.explanation: CONCAT joins the first name, a space and the last name into one display value.

exercises.title: Create a customer location label
exercises.instructions: Combine customer city and postal code using a comma and a space as separator.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT CONCAT_WS(', ', city, postal_code) AS location_label FROM customers;
hints: CONCAT_WS takes the separator first.
exercises.explanation: CONCAT_WS joins the supplied values using the separator and skips NULL arguments.

exercises.title: Build fixed-width course labels
exercises.instructions: For each course, create a label by converting its course ID to text and padding it to three characters with zeroes, then append a hyphen and the course code padded on the right to ten characters with dots.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT CONCAT(LPAD(CAST(course_id AS VARCHAR), 3, '0'), '-', RPAD(course_code, 10, '.')) AS course_label FROM courses;
exercises.hints: Both padding functions operate on text; the numeric ID needs conversion first.
exercises.explanation: CAST converts course_id to text, LPAD and RPAD create fixed-width components, and CONCAT combines them into one label.

exercises.title: Pad project status labels
exercises.instructions: Display each project status padded on the right to a width of 12 using dots.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_status, RPAD(project_status, 12, '.') AS status_label FROM projects;
hints: RPAD adds fill characters on the right.
exercises.explanation: RPAD extends the status text to the requested width with trailing dots.

exercises.title: Normalize employee street labels
exercises.instructions: Display each street in lowercase, remove leading z characters and pad the result on the right to 30 characters using asterisks.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT RPAD(LTRIM(LOWER(street), 'z'), 30, '*') AS formatted_street FROM employees;
hints: Nest the transformations so the innermost function runs first.
exercises.explanation: LOWER runs first, LTRIM removes the leading z characters next, and RPAD adds trailing asterisks.

exercises.title: Replace spaces in product names
exercises.instructions: Show product names with every space replaced by an underscore.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, REPLACE(product_name, ' ', '_') AS compact_name FROM products;
hints: Use REPLACE with a single-space search value.
exercises.explanation: REPLACE substitutes each space with an underscore in the returned text.

exercises.title: Locate the at-sign in customer emails
exercises.instructions: Display each non-missing customer email and the position of its @ character.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT email, POSITION('@' IN email) AS at_position FROM customers WHERE email IS NOT NULL;
hints: Use POSITION for the character location and exclude missing email values.
exercises.explanation: POSITION returns the location of @; the WHERE clause ensures an email value exists.

exercises.title: Extract project code fragments
exercises.instructions: Show each project name and the first four characters of that name, starting at position 1.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, SUBSTR(project_name, 1, 4) AS name_code FROM projects;
hints: SUBSTR starts counting from position 1.
exercises.explanation: The function extracts a four-character prefix from each project name.

exercises.title: Names with optional email
exercises.instructions: Create one label from each employee’s full name and email, separated by a pipe. Missing emails should not create an empty placeholder.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT CONCAT_WS(' | ', CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name), email) AS employee_label FROM employees;
hints: CONCAT_WS skips NULL arguments; build the name as one argument.
exercises.explanation: The inner CONCAT forms the full name and CONCAT_WS joins it to the email only when email is present.

exercises.title: Standardize course titles
exercises.instructions: Display course titles in lowercase and replace every space with a hyphen.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT REPLACE(LOWER(course_title), ' ', '-') AS url_style_title FROM courses;
hints: Apply LOWER before REPLACE.
exercises.explanation: LOWER normalizes letter case; REPLACE changes spaces into hyphens.

exercises.title: Remove repeated prefix characters from SKUs
exercises.instructions: Display each SKU after removing leading C or L characters.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT sku, LTRIM(sku, 'CL') AS shortened_sku FROM products;
hints: LTRIM accepts a set of characters to remove from the left edge.
exercises.explanation: LTRIM strips any leading characters that occur in the supplied character set CL.

exercises.title: Create fixed-width participant names
exercises.instructions: Display participant names padded on the right to 20 characters with periods.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT RPAD(participant_name, 20, '.') AS fixed_name FROM participants;
hints: Use the target width and fill text in RPAD.
exercises.explanation: RPAD returns the name extended with periods to the specified width.

exercises.title: Create formatted student contact strings
exercises.instructions: Display student names as uppercase SURNAME followed by a comma and the lowercase first name.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT CONCAT(UPPER(last_name), ', ', LOWER(first_name)) AS contact_name FROM students;
hints: Combine CONCAT with UPPER and LOWER.
exercises.explanation: The name components are transformed independently and then combined with the comma-space separator.

exercises.title: Compare text lengths in product data
exercises.instructions: Return product names and the length of their descriptions, excluding missing descriptions.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, LENGTH(description) AS description_length FROM products WHERE description IS NOT NULL;
hints: LENGTH counts characters; IS NOT NULL excludes missing values.
exercises.explanation: LENGTH produces the character count for each known description.

exercises.title: Format consultant specialty labels
exercises.instructions: Display consultant specialties with initial capitals and pad them on the left to a width of 14 using underscores.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT LPAD(INITCAP(specialty), 14, '_') AS specialty_label FROM consultants;
hints: Apply INITCAP inside LPAD.
exercises.explanation: INITCAP formats the words first, then LPAD adds leading underscores until the width is 14.

exercises.title: Extract category code prefixes
exercises.instructions: Display category codes and the first three characters of each code.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT category_code, LEFT(category_code, 3) AS code_prefix FROM categories;
hints: LEFT returns the requested number of characters from the start.
exercises.explanation: LEFT with a length of three returns each category code prefix.

exercises.title: Rounded consultant rates
exercises.instructions: Display consultant names and hourly rates rounded to one decimal place.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, ROUND(hourly_rate, 1) AS rounded_rate FROM consultants;
hints: ROUND takes a numeric value and the number of decimal places.
exercises.explanation: ROUND rounds each hourly rate to one decimal place.

exercises.title: Truncated product prices
exercises.instructions: Show product names and prices truncated to one decimal place without rounding.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, TRUNC(unit_price, 1) AS truncated_price FROM products;
hints: TRUNC removes digits beyond the requested decimal place.
exercises.explanation: TRUNC cuts off extra decimals rather than rounding the value.

exercises.title: Even and odd stock quantities
exercises.instructions: Display product names, stock quantities and the remainder when stock is divided by 2.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, stock_quantity, MOD(stock_quantity, 2) AS remainder FROM products;
hints: MOD returns the remainder from division.
exercises.explanation: A remainder of zero indicates an even stock quantity; one indicates an odd quantity.

exercises.title: Calculate discounted course fees
exercises.instructions: Show each course title and its fee after a 10 percent discount.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT course_title, fee * (1 - 0.10) AS discounted_fee FROM courses;
hints: Use arithmetic directly in the SELECT list.
exercises.explanation: Multiplying the fee by 0.90 calculates the amount after a ten percent discount.

exercises.title: Estimate project budget with contingency
exercises.instructions: Display project names and budgets increased by 8 percent.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, budget * 1.08 AS budget_with_contingency FROM projects;
hints: Multiply the existing amount by 1.08.
exercises.explanation: The multiplication adds an eight percent contingency to the original budget.

exercises.title: Rounded order line values
exercises.instructions: For each order line, show the product ID and line amount rounded to two decimal places.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_id, ROUND(quantity * unit_price, 2) AS line_amount FROM order_items;
hints: Multiply quantity by unit price before rounding.
exercises.explanation: The arithmetic calculates the line amount and ROUND formats it to two decimal places.

exercises.title: Truncate project budget to thousands
exercises.instructions: Display each project budget truncated to the nearest thousand.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, TRUNC(budget, -3) AS budget_thousands FROM projects;
hints: A negative precision removes digits to the left of the decimal point.
exercises.explanation: TRUNC with -3 cuts off the final three digits without rounding.

exercises.title: Round student tuition balances
exercises.instructions: Show each enrollment’s student ID and tuition paid rounded to the nearest whole unit.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT student_id, ROUND(tuition_paid, 0) AS rounded_tuition FROM enrollments;
hints: Use zero decimal places for whole-unit rounding.
exercises.explanation: ROUND with precision zero returns a whole-number result for each recorded tuition amount.

exercises.title: Find assignments with whole tens of hours
exercises.instructions: Display project assignment IDs and the remainder when hours worked is divided by 10.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_id, consultant_id, MOD(hours_worked, 10) AS hours_remainder FROM project_assignments;
hints: Use MOD with 10 as the divisor.
exercises.explanation: MOD reports how many hours remain after complete groups of ten hours.

exercises.title: Calculate order item totals
exercises.instructions: Show order ID, product ID and total line value, using the quantity and unit price.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT order_id, product_id, quantity * unit_price AS line_total FROM order_items;
hints: Multiply the two numeric columns.
exercises.explanation: The product of quantity and unit price is the total value for one order line.

exercises.title: Calculate VAT-inclusive product prices
exercises.instructions: Display each product’s current price and a price increased by 21 percent, rounded to two decimal places.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, unit_price, ROUND(unit_price * 1.21, 2) AS price_with_vat FROM products;
hints: Apply the multiplier, then round the result.
exercises.explanation: Multiplying by 1.21 adds 21 percent; ROUND standardizes the displayed decimal precision.

exercises.title: Truncate employee salary to hundreds
exercises.instructions: Display employee names and their salary truncated to the nearest hundred.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, TRUNC(salary, -2) AS salary_hundreds FROM employees;
hints: Use a negative precision of two.
exercises.explanation: TRUNC with -2 removes the tens and units digits without rounding.

exercises.title: Calculate remaining project budget percentage
exercises.instructions: Show project names and the portion of budget remaining after 35 percent has been used.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, budget * (1 - 0.35) AS remaining_budget_estimate FROM projects;
hints: The remaining portion is 1 minus the used fraction.
exercises.explanation: The expression multiplies the budget by 0.65, representing the amount left after 35 percent is spent.

exercises.title: Calculate rounded task costs
exercises.instructions: For each task with recorded hours, estimate its cost using a fixed rate of 85 per hour and display the amount rounded to two decimal places.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT task_id, project_name, ROUND(hours * 85, 2) AS estimated_cost FROM tasks WHERE hours IS NOT NULL;
exercises.hints: Multiply the recorded hours by the stated rate, then round the result.
exercises.explanation: The arithmetic expression calculates a task cost from one row; ROUND formats it to two decimal places. No join is needed because the required values are in tasks.

exercises.title: Show the current date
exercises.instructions: Return today’s date as a single result.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT CURRENT_DATE AS today;
hints: CURRENT_DATE needs no parentheses in the course syntax.
exercises.explanation: CURRENT_DATE returns the database session’s current date.

exercises.title: Show the current time
exercises.instructions: Return the current time as a single result.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT CURRENT_TIME AS time_now;
hints: Use CURRENT_TIME without a table.
exercises.explanation: CURRENT_TIME returns the current time value.

exercises.title: Show the current timestamp
exercises.instructions: Return the current date and time in one result column.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT NOW() AS timestamp_now;
hints: NOW() returns both date and time.
exercises.explanation: NOW() returns the current date-time value.

exercises.title: Employee hire years
exercises.instructions: Display employee names and the year in which each employee was hired.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date) AS hire_year FROM employees;
hints: EXTRACT can retrieve the year component from a date.
exercises.explanation: EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date) returns the year part of each hire date.

exercises.title: Course start months
exercises.instructions: Display each section code and the month number of its start date.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT section_code, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM starts_on) AS start_month FROM class_sections;
hints: Use the MONTH date part.
exercises.explanation: EXTRACT returns the month number from starts_on.

exercises.title: Order day numbers
exercises.instructions: Show each order ID and the day of the month on which it was placed.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT order_id, EXTRACT(DAY FROM order_date) AS order_day FROM orders;
hints: Use EXTRACT with DAY.
exercises.explanation: The result contains the day-of-month component of each order date.

exercises.title: Student ages as intervals
exercises.instructions: Return each student’s name and the interval between their birth date and today.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, AGE(birth_date) AS age_interval FROM students;
hints: AGE(date) calculates the interval from that date to today.
exercises.explanation: AGE returns an interval describing the time elapsed since each student’s birth date.

exercises.title: Months since a fixed date
exercises.instructions: Calculate the month component of the interval between today and 1 September 2021.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT DATE_PART('months', AGE(CURRENT_DATE, TO_DATE('01-09-2021', 'DD-MM-YYYY'))) AS month_part;
hints: Use AGE with two dates and extract the months part with DATE_PART.
exercises.explanation: TO_DATE parses the supplied date, AGE calculates the interval, and DATE_PART returns its month component.

exercises.title: Time between project dates
exercises.instructions: For projects with a recorded end date, show the project name and the interval between start and end dates.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, AGE(end_date, start_date) AS project_duration FROM projects WHERE end_date IS NOT NULL;
hints: AGE can compare two dates; exclude rows without an end date.
exercises.explanation: AGE(end_date, start_date) calculates the interval between the two date values.

exercises.title: Retirement date estimate
exercises.instructions: Display employee names and the date that falls 65 years after each birth date.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, birth_date + INTERVAL '65 years' AS 65th_birthday FROM employees;
hints: Add a year interval to each birth date.
exercises.explanation: The INTERVAL expression shifts each birth date forward by 65 years.

exercises.title: Days since customer registration
exercises.instructions: Show each customer and the number of days between the joining date and today.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, CURRENT_DATE - joined_on AS days_since_joining FROM customers;
hints: Subtract a date column from CURRENT_DATE.
exercises.explanation: Subtracting one date from another returns the number of days between them.

exercises.title: Employees older than thirty
exercises.instructions: Display employees whose age interval is greater than 30 years.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, AGE(birth_date) AS age_interval FROM employees WHERE AGE(birth_date) > '30 years';
hints: Compare the AGE interval with a year interval.
exercises.explanation: AGE calculates an interval and the WHERE condition keeps intervals greater than thirty years.

exercises.title: Student age in whole years
exercises.instructions: Display student names and the whole-year age extracted from each age interval.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM AGE(birth_date)) AS age_years FROM students;
hints: EXTRACT(YEAR FROM AGE(...)) gives whole years.
exercises.explanation: AGE returns an interval; EXTRACT(YEAR) retrieves its year component.

exercises.title: Project schedule components
exercises.instructions: Show project names, start year, start month and start day as separate columns.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM start_date) AS start_year, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM start_date) AS start_month, EXTRACT(DAY FROM start_date) AS start_day FROM projects;
hints: Apply EXTRACT separately for each requested date component.
exercises.explanation: Each EXTRACT expression returns one component of the project start date.

exercises.title: Duration in years from consultant hiring
exercises.instructions: Display consultant names and the year component of the interval since they were hired.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, DATE_PART('year', AGE(CURRENT_DATE, hired_on)) AS years_at_company FROM consultants;
hints: AGE can compare a historical date with CURRENT_DATE; DATE_PART extracts the requested unit.
exercises.explanation: AGE computes the time since hiring, and DATE_PART returns its year component.

exercises.title: Project review date
exercises.instructions: For every project, display its name and a review date calculated as 90 days after the start date.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, start_date + INTERVAL '90 days' AS review_date FROM projects;
hints: Add an interval to a date value.
exercises.explanation: Adding a 90-day interval produces a review date for each project.

exercises.title: Employee ID as text
exercises.instructions: Display employee IDs converted to text alongside employee names.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT CAST(employee_id AS VARCHAR) AS employee_code, first_name, last_name FROM employees;
hints: Use CAST with the target type.
exercises.explanation: CAST converts the integer identifier into a character value for display.

exercises.title: Format customer join dates
exercises.instructions: Display customer names and join dates in DD-MM-YYYY format.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, TO_CHAR(joined_on, 'DD-MM-YYYY') AS joined_display FROM customers;
hints: TO_CHAR converts a date into text using the supplied format.
exercises.explanation: The format pattern prints a two-digit day, two-digit month and four-digit year.

exercises.title: Parse a supplied date
exercises.instructions: Convert the text 29-10-2021 into a date value using its day-month-year pattern.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT TO_DATE('29-10-2021', 'DD-MM-YYYY') AS parsed_date;
hints: TO_DATE requires a format that matches the text and includes the year.
exercises.explanation: TO_DATE interprets the supplied string as a date according to DD-MM-YYYY.

exercises.title: Convert a text amount to a number
exercises.instructions: Convert the text value 2500 to a number using a four-digit numeric format.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT TO_NUMBER('2500', '9999') AS amount;
hints: Use TO_NUMBER with a format matching the text.
exercises.explanation: TO_NUMBER parses the text and returns a numeric value.

exercises.title: Convert customer postal codes to integers
exercises.instructions: Display customer IDs and postal codes converted to integer values.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT customer_id, postal_code::INTEGER AS postal_code_number FROM customers;
hints: PostgreSQL supports the ::type shorthand.
exercises.explanation: The shorthand casts each text postal code to an integer; leading zeroes are not preserved in the numeric result.

exercises.title: Format project budgets as text
exercises.instructions: Display project names and budgets converted to text with two decimal places.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, TO_CHAR(budget, '9999999.99') AS budget_text FROM projects;
hints: TO_CHAR accepts a numeric value and a numeric format.
exercises.explanation: The format converts the numeric budget into a text representation with two decimal places.

exercises.title: Display section dates with month names
exercises.instructions: Show section codes and dates using day number, full month name and year, with month padding removed.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT section_code, TO_CHAR(starts_on, 'DD FMMonth YYYY') AS start_display FROM class_sections;
hints: FM removes padding spaces from month names.
exercises.explanation: TO_CHAR formats the date, and FM prevents the full month name from being padded with spaces.

exercises.title: Convert a numeric product price to integer
exercises.instructions: Display product names and their prices converted to integer values.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_name, CAST(unit_price AS INTEGER) AS whole_price FROM products;
hints: CAST changes the value to the requested numeric type.
exercises.explanation: CAST converts the numeric price to an integer result.

exercises.title: Parse a year-first date string
exercises.instructions: Convert the text 2021-10-29 into a date using a year-month-day format.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT TO_DATE('2021-10-29', 'YYYY-MM-DD') AS parsed_date;
hints: Use a format mask that follows the same order as the text.
exercises.explanation: TO_DATE parses the year, month and day components using YYYY-MM-DD.

exercises.title: Display dates with abbreviated weekday
exercises.instructions: Display project start dates with a three-letter weekday followed by day, month and year.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_name, TO_CHAR(start_date, 'dy DD-MM-YYYY') AS start_label FROM projects;
hints: Use dy for a short weekday name.
exercises.explanation: TO_CHAR formats the date into the requested abbreviated weekday and numeric date components.

exercises.title: Format a date without padded month text
exercises.instructions: Display employee birth dates as day, full month and year without the extra spaces that Month can add.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, TO_CHAR(birth_date, 'DD FMMonth YYYY') AS birth_display FROM employees;
hints: Prefix Month with FM to suppress padding.
exercises.explanation: FM removes the padding spaces that the Month template may add.

exercises.title: Format a calculated age milestone date
exercises.instructions: Display student names and the date 30 years after birth in DD-MM-YYYY text format.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT first_name, last_name, TO_CHAR(birth_date + INTERVAL '30 years', 'DD-MM-YYYY') AS milestone_date FROM students;
hints: First calculate the date using INTERVAL, then convert that date to text.
exercises.explanation: The interval addition creates the milestone date, and TO_CHAR formats the calculated date.

exercises.title: What LENGTH returns
exercises.instructions: What does LENGTH(text) return?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: The position of the first space
exercises.explanation: LENGTH counts the characters in its text argument.

exercises.title: ROUND versus TRUNC
exercises.instructions: Which statement correctly describes TRUNC(number, 2)?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: It removes digits after two decimal places without rounding
It converts the number to text
exercises.explanation: TRUNC cuts off extra decimal places without rounding the value.

exercises.title: AGE result type
exercises.instructions: What kind of result does AGE(date) produce?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: An integer count of days only
exercises.explanation: AGE returns an interval describing the elapsed time from the supplied date to today.

exercises.title: Purpose of TO_DATE
exercises.instructions: What does TO_DATE(text, format) do?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: Converts text into a date using a format
Rounds a date to the nearest month
exercises.explanation: TO_DATE parses text into a date according to the supplied format pattern.

exercises.title: Purpose of CONCAT_WS
exercises.instructions: What is a distinguishing behavior of CONCAT_WS(separator, ...)?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: It converts all text to uppercase
It returns the length of the result
exercises.explanation: CONCAT_WS joins arguments using a separator and skips NULL arguments.

exercises.title: Meaning of EXTRACT
exercises.instructions: Which expression retrieves the month number from a date column named start_date?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.explanation: EXTRACT(MONTH FROM date) returns the month component as a numeric value.

exercises.title: MOD result
exercises.instructions: What does MOD(17, 5) return?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.explanation: MOD returns the remainder after division; 17 divided by 5 leaves a remainder of 2.

exercises.title: Employee department directory
exercises.instructions: Display each employee’s name together with the name of the department to which the employee belongs.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, d.department_name FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
hints: Join employees to departments using their shared department identifier.
exercises.explanation: The INNER JOIN returns employees whose department ID matches a department row.

exercises.title: Department office cities
exercises.instructions: Show department names and the cities in which their offices are located.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT d.department_name, l.city FROM departments d JOIN locations l ON d.location_id = l.location_id;
hints: The department table stores the location ID.
exercises.explanation: The join connects each department to its matching location record.

exercises.title: Course section overview
exercises.instructions: Display each section code together with the title of its course.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT s.section_code, c.course_title FROM class_sections s JOIN courses c ON s.course_id = c.course_id;
hints: Match a section to its course using course_id.
exercises.explanation: The join returns section rows with their corresponding course titles.

exercises.title: Teacher section assignments
exercises.instructions: List each teacher’s first and last name alongside the section codes they teach.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT t.first_name, t.last_name, s.section_code FROM teachers t JOIN class_sections s ON t.teacher_id = s.teacher_id;
hints: Use the teacher identifier stored in class_sections.
exercises.explanation: The INNER JOIN matches each section with its assigned teacher.

exercises.title: Customer order dates
exercises.instructions: Show customer names and the dates of their orders.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, o.order_date FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
hints: Connect customers to their orders through customer_id.
exercises.explanation: Each returned row represents a customer-order match.

exercises.title: Product category labels

exercises.title: Project client list

exercises.title: Consultant assignment roles

exercises.hints: The assignment connects a consultant to a project; the project identifies its client.

exercises.title: Training session leaders

exercises.explanation: The join enriches each session with the trainer’s name.

exercises.title: Student enrollment dates

exercises.hints: Start from enrollment records and follow both parts of the section key before retrieving the course title.

exercises.title: Employee task assignment names

exercises.title: Products and their category codes

exercises.title: Department locations by country

exercises.hints: Follow the employee-to-department relationship and then the department-to-location relationship.
exercises.explanation: The first join finds each employee’s department; the second uses the department’s location_id to retrieve its country.

exercises.title: Clients and project statuses
exercises.instructions: Display client names and the status of each project they have commissioned.

hints: The relationship is clients to projects by client_id.
exercises.explanation: The query returns matching client and project records.

exercises.title: Sections with their teacher email
exercises.instructions: Display section codes and the email addresses of their assigned teachers.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT s.section_code, t.email FROM class_sections s JOIN teachers t ON s.teacher_id = t.teacher_id;
hints: Connect the section’s teacher ID to teachers.
exercises.explanation: The join retrieves the teacher email for each section with an assigned teacher.

exercises.title: Customers and order status
exercises.instructions: Show customer names, order IDs and order statuses for every matching order.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, o.order_id, o.order_status FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
hints: The order table contains the matching customer ID.
exercises.explanation: The INNER JOIN includes customers only when at least one order matches.

exercises.title: Employee task project listing
exercises.instructions: Display employee names, task names and project names for all recorded tasks.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, t.task_name, t.project_name FROM tasks t JOIN employees e ON t.employee_id = e.employee_id;
hints: The task record links to an employee through employee_id.
exercises.explanation: The join adds employee identity to each task row.

exercises.title: Student course enrollment report
exercises.instructions: Display student names, course titles and final grades for each enrollment.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT st.first_name, st.last_name, c.course_title, e.final_grade FROM enrollments e JOIN students st ON e.student_id = st.student_id JOIN courses c ON e.course_id = c.course_id;
hints: The enrollment table links to both student and course records.
exercises.explanation: Two joins retrieve the student and course details for each enrollment.

exercises.title: Section teacher and course report
exercises.instructions: Show section codes, course titles and teacher names.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT s.section_code, c.course_title, t.first_name, t.last_name FROM class_sections s JOIN courses c ON s.course_id = c.course_id JOIN teachers t ON s.teacher_id = t.teacher_id;
hints: A section links separately to a course and a teacher.
exercises.explanation: The query follows both foreign-key relationships from class_sections.

exercises.title: Detailed retail order lines
exercises.instructions: Display order ID, order date, customer name, product name and quantity for every order line.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date, c.first_name, c.last_name, p.product_name, oi.quantity FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id;
hints: Follow the order to its customer and line items, then each line to its product.
exercises.explanation: The chain of INNER JOINs connects an order to a customer, order lines and products.

exercises.title: Retail product category and line quantities
