exercises.instructions: Show product names, category names and quantities sold on each order line.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.product_name, c.category_name, oi.quantity FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id;
hints: The product connects order_items to categories.
exercises.explanation: The joins retrieve product and category descriptions for each order line.

exercises.title: Consultant project and client details
exercises.instructions: Display consultant names, project names, client names and assignment roles.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, p.project_name, cl.client_name, a.role_name FROM project_assignments a JOIN consultants c ON a.consultant_id = c.consultant_id JOIN projects p ON a.project_id = p.project_id JOIN clients cl ON p.client_id = cl.client_id;
hints: The assignment connects a consultant to a project; the project connects to a client.
exercises.explanation: The joins follow both sides of the assignment and then retrieve the project’s client.

exercises.title: Training attendees and trainers
exercises.instructions: Display participant names, session titles and trainer names for participants registered for a session.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.participant_name, s.session_title, c.first_name, c.last_name FROM participants p JOIN training_sessions s ON p.session_id = s.session_id JOIN consultants c ON s.trainer_id = c.consultant_id;
hints: Connect participant to session, then session to trainer.
exercises.explanation: The two joins retrieve the session and trainer associated with each participant.

exercises.title: Employee task with department location
exercises.instructions: Display employee names, department names, city and task names for employees who have a department and a task.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, d.department_name, l.city, t.task_name FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id JOIN locations l ON d.location_id = l.location_id JOIN tasks t ON e.employee_id = t.employee_id;
hints: Follow employee to department, department to location and employee to tasks.
exercises.explanation: The query joins all four tables through their matching key columns.

exercises.title: Course enrollment with teacher
exercises.instructions: Show student names, course titles, section codes and teacher names for all enrolled students.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT st.first_name, st.last_name, c.course_title, s.section_code, t.first_name AS teacher_first_name, t.last_name AS teacher_last_name FROM enrollments e JOIN students st ON e.student_id = st.student_id JOIN class_sections s ON e.section_id = s.section_id AND e.course_id = s.course_id JOIN courses c ON s.course_id = c.course_id JOIN teachers t ON s.teacher_id = t.teacher_id;
hints: Follow the enrollment to student and matching section, then to the course and teacher.
exercises.explanation: The query uses the section relationship and retrieves the course and teacher details for each enrollment.

exercises.title: Order shipping location and product details
exercises.instructions: Display order ID, shipping city, product name and quantity for all ordered products.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT o.order_id, o.shipping_city, p.product_name, oi.quantity FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id;
hints: Join orders to their line items, then to products.
exercises.explanation: The joins connect order headers with individual products on each line.

exercises.title: Project staffing with consultant specialty
exercises.instructions: Display project names, consultant names and specialties for assigned consultants.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.project_name, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.specialty FROM projects p JOIN project_assignments a ON p.project_id = a.project_id JOIN consultants c ON a.consultant_id = c.consultant_id;
hints: The assignments table links the two main entities.
exercises.explanation: The joins connect each project to its assignments and each assignment to a consultant.

exercises.title: Product price by order and customer
exercises.instructions: Display customer names, order dates, product names and the unit prices charged on each order line.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, o.order_date, p.product_name, oi.unit_price FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id;
hints: Follow customers to orders, order lines and products.
exercises.explanation: The chain returns customer, order and product details alongside the recorded order-line price.

exercises.title: Teacher salary and enrolled course
exercises.instructions: Display teacher names, course titles and annual salaries for courses with a section assigned to a teacher.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT t.first_name, t.last_name, c.course_title, t.annual_salary FROM teachers t JOIN class_sections s ON t.teacher_id = s.teacher_id JOIN courses c ON s.course_id = c.course_id;
hints: A teacher connects to sections, which connect to courses.
exercises.explanation: The joins retrieve the course taught by each teacher and the teacher’s salary.

exercises.title: Match enrollments to exact class sections
exercises.instructions: Display student IDs, section codes and course IDs for enrollment records, matching enrollments to their exact section rows.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.student_id, s.section_code, e.course_id FROM enrollments e JOIN class_sections s ON e.section_id = s.section_id AND e.course_id = s.course_id;
hints: The class section key consists of both section_id and course_id.
exercises.explanation: Both key columns are required to match the correct class section because section_id can repeat across courses.

exercises.title: Student grades with section start dates
exercises.instructions: Show student IDs, section codes, registration dates and section start dates for each enrollment.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.student_id, s.section_code, e.registered_on, s.starts_on FROM enrollments e JOIN class_sections s ON e.section_id = s.section_id AND e.course_id = s.course_id;
hints: Use both columns from the composite section key in the ON condition.
exercises.explanation: The two-column join ensures that each enrollment is associated with the correct section-course combination.

exercises.title: Class section room assignments
exercises.instructions: Display each section code, course ID, room code and building by matching the section to its room record.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT s.section_code, s.course_id, r.room_code, r.building FROM class_sections s JOIN section_rooms r ON s.section_id = r.section_id AND s.course_id = r.course_id;
hints: The room record is identified by the same two columns as the class section.
exercises.explanation: Both section_id and course_id are required in the ON condition so the room is matched to the exact section-course pair.

exercises.title: Enrollment and section capacity
exercises.instructions: Display each student enrollment alongside the seat limit of the exact section.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.student_id, e.section_id, e.course_id, s.seat_limit FROM enrollments e JOIN class_sections s ON e.section_id = s.section_id AND e.course_id = s.course_id;
hints: Match both components of the section primary key.
exercises.explanation: Both section_id and course_id are necessary to retrieve the right seat limit.

exercises.title: Reviewed project assignments
exercises.instructions: Display project names, consultant names, review dates and review notes for assignments that have a recorded review.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.project_name, c.first_name, c.last_name, r.reviewed_on, r.review_note FROM project_assignments a JOIN assignment_reviews r ON a.project_id = r.project_id AND a.consultant_id = r.consultant_id JOIN projects p ON a.project_id = p.project_id JOIN consultants c ON a.consultant_id = c.consultant_id;
hints: Match the review to an assignment using both project_id and consultant_id.
exercises.explanation: The assignment and review tables share the composite assignment key; both columns must match before the project and consultant details are retrieved.

exercises.title: List exact section registrations for one course
exercises.instructions: For course 301, display student IDs and section codes, ensuring each registration is linked to the correct section for that course.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.student_id, s.section_code FROM enrollments e JOIN class_sections s ON e.section_id = s.section_id AND e.course_id = s.course_id WHERE e.course_id = 301;
hints: Join using both section key columns, then apply the course filter.
exercises.explanation: The composite join matches both section ID and course ID before the course-specific filter is applied.

exercises.title: Enrollment room lookup
exercises.instructions: Display student IDs, room codes and buildings for enrollments matched to their exact class-section room records.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.student_id, r.room_code, r.building FROM enrollments e JOIN section_rooms r ON e.section_id = r.section_id AND e.course_id = r.course_id;
hints: Use both section_id and course_id to match the composite room key.
exercises.explanation: The composite join associates each enrollment with the room belonging to its exact section-course pair.

exercises.title: Assignment review history with consultant
exercises.instructions: Display project IDs, consultant names, review dates and notes for each reviewed assignment.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT a.project_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, r.reviewed_on, r.review_note FROM project_assignments a JOIN assignment_reviews r ON a.project_id = r.project_id AND a.consultant_id = r.consultant_id JOIN consultants c ON a.consultant_id = c.consultant_id;
hints: The review table refers to an assignment through the two-column project-consultant key.
exercises.explanation: The two key columns match each review to its assignment before the consultant details are returned.

exercises.title: Classify products by price band
exercises.instructions: Display product names, prices and the label of the price band into which each product falls.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.product_name, p.unit_price, b.band_label FROM products p JOIN price_bands b ON p.unit_price >= b.min_price AND p.unit_price <= b.max_price;
hints: The price must be between the band’s lower and upper values.
exercises.explanation: The non-equi join uses two range comparisons to match each product to its corresponding price band.

exercises.title: Assign budget categories to projects
exercises.instructions: Show project names, budgets and the budget-band name that covers each project budget.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.project_name, p.budget, b.band_name FROM projects p JOIN budget_bands b ON p.budget >= b.min_budget AND p.budget <= b.max_budget;
hints: The project budget is matched against a minimum and maximum range.
exercises.explanation: The two comparison conditions define the budget interval that contains each project.

exercises.title: Find products in the standard band
exercises.instructions: Display product names and prices for products that match the Standard price band.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.product_name, p.unit_price FROM products p JOIN price_bands b ON p.unit_price >= b.min_price AND p.unit_price <= b.max_price WHERE b.band_label = 'Standard';
hints: Use a range join and then filter the band label.
exercises.explanation: The non-equi join assigns products to price ranges and WHERE keeps the Standard band.

exercises.title: Find projects with large budgets
exercises.instructions: Display the names and budgets of projects that fall into the Large budget band.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.project_name, p.budget FROM projects p JOIN budget_bands b ON p.budget >= b.min_budget AND p.budget <= b.max_budget WHERE b.band_name = 'Large';
hints: Join on the budget range, then filter by the band label.
exercises.explanation: The range comparison identifies the band and the label condition retains Large projects.

exercises.title: Classify low and medium product prices
exercises.instructions: Return product names, prices and band labels for products priced at no more than 100.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.product_name, p.unit_price, b.band_label FROM products p JOIN price_bands b ON p.unit_price >= b.min_price AND p.unit_price <= b.max_price WHERE p.unit_price <= 100 ORDER BY p.unit_price;
hints: Use both range boundaries in the join and an additional price filter.
exercises.explanation: The join maps each product to a range; WHERE limits the result to products costing at most 100.

exercises.title: Compare project budgets to all fitting bands
exercises.instructions: Display project names, budget values and budget band labels for projects in the Medium or Large ranges.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.project_name, p.budget, b.band_name FROM projects p JOIN budget_bands b ON p.budget >= b.min_budget AND p.budget <= b.max_budget WHERE b.band_name IN ('Medium', 'Large');
hints: Use the non-equi range match followed by an IN condition.
exercises.explanation: The join matches budgets to bands, and the filter keeps the two requested band labels.

exercises.title: Price bands for high-value products
exercises.instructions: Show product names and price-band labels for products whose price is at least 150.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.product_name, p.unit_price, b.band_label FROM products p JOIN price_bands b ON p.unit_price >= b.min_price AND p.unit_price <= b.max_price WHERE p.unit_price >= 150;
hints: A range join can be combined with a regular WHERE condition.
exercises.explanation: The range join finds the band for each price; WHERE then retains products at or above the threshold.

exercises.title: Find projects within their assigned spend class
exercises.instructions: Display project ID, project name, budget and band name ordered from lowest budget to highest.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.project_id, p.project_name, p.budget, b.band_name FROM projects p JOIN budget_bands b ON p.budget >= b.min_budget AND p.budget <= b.max_budget ORDER BY p.budget;
hints: Match the budget to the correct range and sort the result by budget.
exercises.explanation: The range join classifies every project budget; ORDER BY sorts the matched projects from low to high.

exercises.title: Employee and direct manager names
exercises.instructions: Display each employee’s surname alongside the surname of their direct manager.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.last_name AS employee, m.last_name AS manager FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;
hints: Use employees twice with different aliases.
exercises.explanation: The first alias represents the employee and the second alias represents the manager.

exercises.title: Consultant and manager specialties
exercises.instructions: Show each consultant’s name and their manager’s specialty.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, m.specialty AS manager_specialty FROM consultants c JOIN consultants m ON c.manager_id = m.consultant_id;
hints: Join the consultant table to itself through manager_id.
exercises.explanation: The second consultant alias represents the manager row referenced by the first row.

exercises.title: Employees hired in the same month
exercises.instructions: List pairs of different employees who were hired in the same calendar month. Show both surnames and the month number.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e1.last_name AS employee_one, e2.last_name AS employee_two, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM e1.hire_date) AS hire_month FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON EXTRACT(MONTH FROM e1.hire_date) = EXTRACT(MONTH FROM e2.hire_date) AND e1.employee_id < e2.employee_id;
hints: Compare month parts and use an ordering condition on employee IDs to list each pair once.
exercises.explanation: The self join matches equal hire months; the < condition prevents self-pairs and duplicate reversed pairs.

exercises.title: Consultants with the same specialty
exercises.instructions: Find pairs of distinct consultants who share the same specialty. Display both names and the specialty.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c1.first_name, c1.last_name, c2.first_name AS colleague_first_name, c2.last_name AS colleague_last_name, c1.specialty FROM consultants c1 JOIN consultants c2 ON c1.specialty = c2.specialty AND c1.consultant_id < c2.consultant_id;
hints: Join the table to itself on specialty and keep one direction of each pair.
exercises.explanation: The specialty condition finds related rows and the ID comparison avoids repeated pair orderings.

exercises.title: Employees who share a department
exercises.instructions: List pairs of employees who work in the same department, displaying both employee IDs and the department ID.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e1.employee_id, e2.employee_id AS colleague_id, e1.department_id FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.department_id = e2.department_id AND e1.employee_id < e2.employee_id;
hints: Use the department ID as the match condition and compare IDs to avoid duplicates.
exercises.explanation: The self join pairs employees in the same department and retains each pair once.

exercises.title: Projects for the same client
exercises.instructions: Display pairs of different projects commissioned by the same client, together with the client ID.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p1.project_name, p2.project_name AS other_project, p1.client_id FROM projects p1 JOIN projects p2 ON p1.client_id = p2.client_id AND p1.project_id < p2.project_id;
hints: Join projects on client_id and keep one ordering of each pair.
exercises.explanation: Projects are related when they have the same client; the ID comparison removes self-pairs and duplicate pair directions.

exercises.title: Students living in the same city
exercises.instructions: List pairs of different students who live in the same city. Display both student IDs and the city.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT s1.student_id, s2.student_id AS other_student_id, s1.city FROM students s1 JOIN students s2 ON s1.city = s2.city AND s1.student_id < s2.student_id;
hints: Compare city values and retain only one order for each pair.
exercises.explanation: The self join finds matching city values and the < condition lists each pair once.

exercises.title: Consultants hired in the same year
exercises.instructions: Display pairs of consultants hired in the same year, including both surnames and the hiring year.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c1.last_name, c2.last_name AS colleague_last_name, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM c1.hired_on) AS hired_year FROM consultants c1 JOIN consultants c2 ON EXTRACT(YEAR FROM c1.hired_on) = EXTRACT(YEAR FROM c2.hired_on) AND c1.consultant_id < c2.consultant_id;
hints: Compare the year extracted from each hire date.
exercises.explanation: The join pairs consultants hired in the same year; the ID comparison removes repeated pairings.

exercises.title: Employees with a more highly paid colleague
exercises.instructions: Find employee pairs in the same department where one employee earns more than the other. Display both names and both salaries.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e1.first_name, e1.last_name, e1.salary, e2.first_name AS colleague_first_name, e2.last_name AS colleague_last_name, e2.salary AS colleague_salary FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.department_id = e2.department_id AND e1.salary > e2.salary;
hints: Use one copy of the table for each side of the comparison.
exercises.explanation: The join matches employees in the same department and keeps pairs where the first salary is greater than the second.

exercises.title: Employee, manager and manager’s manager
exercises.instructions: Display employee surnames, manager surnames and the surnames of each manager’s manager.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.last_name AS employee, m.last_name AS manager, g.last_name AS manager_of_manager FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id JOIN employees g ON m.manager_id = g.employee_id;
hints: Use three aliases for the three levels of the hierarchy.
exercises.explanation: The first join finds the direct manager; the second follows the manager’s own manager_id to the next level.

exercises.title: Consultant hierarchy two levels deep
exercises.instructions: Show consultant, manager and manager-of-manager names where both hierarchy links exist.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.last_name AS consultant, m.last_name AS manager, g.last_name AS manager_of_manager FROM consultants c JOIN consultants m ON c.manager_id = m.consultant_id JOIN consultants g ON m.manager_id = g.consultant_id;
hints: Follow manager_id twice using separate aliases.
exercises.explanation: The two self joins trace the consultant’s manager and then the manager’s manager.

exercises.title: Employees sharing a birth month
exercises.instructions: List all ordered employee pairs who share a birth month, allowing both pair directions to appear.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e1.last_name AS employee_one, e2.last_name AS employee_two FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON EXTRACT(MONTH FROM e1.birth_date) = EXTRACT(MONTH FROM e2.birth_date) AND e1.employee_id <> e2.employee_id;
hints: Use a not-equal test rather than a less-than test to keep both directions.
exercises.explanation: The join matches the birth month and excludes pairing a row with itself; <> allows each pair to appear in both directions.

exercises.title: Consultants with a higher rate than their manager
exercises.instructions: Display consultants whose hourly rate is greater than the rate of their direct manager, with both rates.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, c.hourly_rate, m.first_name AS manager_first_name, m.last_name AS manager_last_name, m.hourly_rate AS manager_rate FROM consultants c JOIN consultants m ON c.manager_id = m.consultant_id WHERE c.hourly_rate > m.hourly_rate;
hints: Join the employee row to its manager row, then compare the two rates.
exercises.explanation: The self join retrieves the direct manager’s rate; WHERE keeps consultants whose rate exceeds it.

exercises.title: Projects sharing a start month and client
exercises.instructions: Find pairs of different projects for the same client that started in the same month.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p1.project_name, p2.project_name AS related_project, p1.client_id, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM p1.start_date) AS start_month FROM projects p1 JOIN projects p2 ON p1.client_id = p2.client_id AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM p1.start_date) = EXTRACT(MONTH FROM p2.start_date) AND p1.project_id < p2.project_id;
hints: Combine the same-client condition with a month comparison and a one-direction pair condition.
exercises.explanation: All three ON conditions must hold: same client, same start month and different project IDs in a consistent order.

exercises.title: Employees in the same department with different hire dates
exercises.instructions: Show pairs of employees in the same department where the first employee was hired before the second employee.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e1.last_name AS earlier_hire, e2.last_name AS later_hire, e1.department_id FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.department_id = e2.department_id AND e1.hire_date < e2.hire_date;
hints: Compare the hire dates while matching department IDs.
exercises.explanation: The join condition requires both a shared department and an earlier hire date for the first employee.

exercises.title: Participants registered on the same date
exercises.instructions: List pairs of distinct participants who registered on the same date, showing both names and the date.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p1.participant_name, p2.participant_name AS other_participant, p1.registered_on FROM participants p1 JOIN participants p2 ON p1.registered_on = p2.registered_on AND p1.participant_id < p2.participant_id;
hints: Use registered_on to find the same-date pairs.
exercises.explanation: The self join compares registrations by date and uses IDs so each pair is returned once.

exercises.title: What INNER JOIN keeps
exercises.instructions: Which rows are returned by an INNER JOIN?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: Every row from the left table
Every row from the right table
Only rows with matching join values in both tables
All rows from both tables, matched or unmatched
exercises.explanation: INNER JOIN returns only rows for which the join condition finds a match in both tables.

exercises.title: Purpose of ON
exercises.instructions: What is the purpose of the ON clause in a JOIN?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: To define how rows from the tables match
To limit the final row count
exercises.explanation: ON specifies the relationship condition used to match rows from the joined tables.

exercises.title: Joining several tables
exercises.instructions: When joining three related tables, what should connect each additional table?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: A matching relationship expressed with JOIN and ON
exercises.explanation: Each additional table should be joined through the relevant key relationship using JOIN ... ON.

exercises.title: Composite key matching
exercises.instructions: A relationship uses a two-column composite key. What should the join condition normally include?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: Both key columns connected with AND
A text concatenation of the two columns
exercises.explanation: All required columns of the composite key must be matched, typically with AND.

exercises.title: Why aliases in a self join
exercises.instructions: Why does a self join use two different table aliases?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: To represent separate roles for the two occurrences of the same table
To convert a table into a view
exercises.explanation: Different aliases let the query refer to each occurrence of the same table independently.

exercises.title: Recognizing a non-equi join
exercises.instructions: Which condition is an example of a non-equi join?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.explanation: A range join uses comparison operators to match a value to minimum and maximum bounds.

exercises.title: List each pair once
exercises.instructions: In a self join that finds related pairs, why might a query use e1.id < e2.id?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: To prevent self-pairs and duplicate reversed pairs
exercises.explanation: A strict less-than condition selects one direction of each distinct pair and excludes pairing a row with itself.

exercises.title: Avoiding ambiguous columns
exercises.instructions: When two joined tables contain a column with the same name, what is the clearest way to refer to it?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: Prefix it with the table alias
exercises.explanation: Qualifying a column with its table alias prevents ambiguity and makes the source clear.

exercises.title: Count all employees
exercises.instructions: Return the total number of employee records.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS employee_count FROM employees;
hints: COUNT(*) includes every row.
exercises.explanation: COUNT(*) counts all rows regardless of whether individual columns contain NULL.

exercises.title: Count employees with email addresses
exercises.instructions: Return the number of employees whose email address is recorded.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT COUNT(email) AS employees_with_email FROM employees;
hints: COUNT(column) ignores NULL values in that column.
exercises.explanation: COUNT(email) counts only rows where email is not NULL.

exercises.title: Count distinct customer cities
exercises.instructions: Return the number of different non-NULL cities represented in the customer table.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS city_count FROM customers;
hints: Combine COUNT with DISTINCT on the column.
exercises.explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT city) counts each distinct non-NULL city value once.

exercises.title: Total retail stock
exercises.instructions: Calculate the total number of units currently in stock across all products.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT SUM(stock_quantity) AS total_stock FROM products;
hints: Use SUM on the numeric stock column.
exercises.explanation: SUM adds all non-NULL stock quantities into one result.

exercises.title: Average course fee
exercises.instructions: Calculate the average fee across all courses.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT AVG(fee) AS average_course_fee FROM courses;
hints: AVG returns the arithmetic mean of numeric values.
exercises.explanation: AVG calculates the mean course fee across the course rows.

exercises.title: Lowest and highest consultant rates
exercises.instructions: Return the minimum and maximum hourly rates among consultants.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT MIN(hourly_rate) AS lowest_rate, MAX(hourly_rate) AS highest_rate FROM consultants;
hints: Use MIN and MAX on the same numeric column.
exercises.explanation: MIN finds the smallest rate and MAX finds the largest rate.

exercises.title: Oldest and newest order dates
exercises.instructions: Return the earliest and latest dates recorded in the orders table.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT MIN(order_date) AS first_order, MAX(order_date) AS latest_order FROM orders;
hints: MIN and MAX also work with date values.
exercises.explanation: The aggregate functions compare dates and return the earliest and latest order dates.

exercises.title: Count enrollments with a recorded grade
exercises.instructions: Return the number of enrollments with a non-NULL final grade.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT COUNT(final_grade) AS graded_enrollments FROM enrollments;
hints: COUNT(column) excludes missing grades.
exercises.explanation: The aggregate counts only enrollment rows with a recorded final_grade.

exercises.title: Compare all enrollments with graded enrollments
exercises.instructions: Return both the total number of enrollment rows and the number with a recorded final grade.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_enrollments, COUNT(final_grade) AS graded_enrollments FROM enrollments;
hints: Use COUNT(*) and COUNT(final_grade) side by side.
exercises.explanation: COUNT(*) counts every enrollment; COUNT(final_grade) ignores rows with a NULL grade.

exercises.title: Total value of all order lines
exercises.instructions: Calculate the combined value of all order lines using quantity multiplied by the charged unit price.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS total_order_value FROM order_items;
hints: The aggregate can contain an arithmetic expression.
exercises.explanation: The expression calculates each line value and SUM adds those values together.

exercises.title: Average task hours
exercises.instructions: Calculate the average recorded task hours, ignoring tasks where hours are missing.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT AVG(hours) AS average_task_hours FROM tasks;
hints: AVG ignores NULL values automatically.
exercises.explanation: AVG calculates the mean of known hours values and does not treat NULL as zero.

exercises.title: Alphabetically first and last course titles
exercises.instructions: Return the alphabetically first and last course titles.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT MIN(course_title) AS first_title, MAX(course_title) AS last_title FROM courses;
hints: MIN and MAX also compare text values alphabetically.
exercises.explanation: The aggregate functions return the first and last text values in the sort order.

exercises.title: Average surname length
exercises.instructions: Return the average number of characters in employee surnames, rounded to the nearest whole number.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT ROUND(AVG(LENGTH(last_name))) AS average_surname_length FROM employees;
hints: Calculate a text length for each row before averaging.
exercises.explanation: LENGTH produces one numeric value per surname, AVG calculates the mean and ROUND rounds it to a whole number.

exercises.title: Count products with unique category assignments
exercises.instructions: Return the number of different non-NULL category IDs represented in products.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT category_id) AS represented_categories FROM products;
hints: Count distinct values rather than product rows.
exercises.explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT category_id) counts each represented category once and ignores NULL category IDs.

exercises.title: Total consultant assignment hours
exercises.instructions: Calculate the total recorded hours across all project assignments.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT SUM(hours_worked) AS total_assignment_hours FROM project_assignments;
hints: SUM adds non-NULL numeric values.
exercises.explanation: The aggregate returns one total across the assignment table, ignoring any missing hour values.

exercises.title: Training duration range
exercises.instructions: Among training sessions held on or after 1 January 2025, return the shortest and longest session durations.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT MIN(duration_hours) AS shortest_session, MAX(duration_hours) AS longest_session FROM training_sessions WHERE session_date >= '2025-01-01';
exercises.hints: Filter the session rows before calculating the two aggregate values.
exercises.explanation: WHERE limits the rows to sessions on or after the date; MIN and MAX then return the duration boundaries for that subset.

exercises.title: Count orders placed by all customers combined
exercises.instructions: Count the retail orders whose status is either Processing or Shipped.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE order_status IN ('Processing', 'Shipped');
exercises.hints: Filter the order rows to the two requested status values before counting.
exercises.explanation: IN keeps orders whose status matches either listed value; COUNT(*) counts all qualifying order rows.

exercises.title: Employees per department
exercises.instructions: Show each department ID and the number of employees assigned to it.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS employee_count FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;
hints: Group employee rows by department before counting them.
exercises.explanation: GROUP BY creates one group per department_id and COUNT(*) counts rows within each group.

exercises.title: Products per category
exercises.instructions: Display each category ID and the number of products in that category.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT category_id, COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category_id;
hints: Use category_id as the grouping column.
exercises.explanation: Each category forms a group, and COUNT(*) returns its product count.

exercises.title: Orders per customer
exercises.instructions: Show customer IDs and the number of orders placed by each customer who has at least one order.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
hints: Group orders by customer ID.
exercises.explanation: GROUP BY returns one row per customer represented in orders, with a count for each customer.

exercises.title: Average grade per course
exercises.instructions: For every course with at least one enrollment, display its ID, title, enrollment count and average recorded grade.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.course_id, c.course_title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrollment_count, AVG(e.final_grade) AS average_grade FROM courses c JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id GROUP BY c.course_id, c.course_title;
exercises.hints: Join the course information to enrollments, then group by the course fields shown in the result.
exercises.explanation: The join associates enrollment rows with course titles. GROUP BY creates one course group; COUNT counts enrollment records and AVG ignores NULL grades.

exercises.title: Total stock by category
exercises.instructions: Show category IDs and the total stock quantity of products in each category.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT category_id, SUM(stock_quantity) AS category_stock FROM products GROUP BY category_id;
hints: SUM calculates the stock total within each category.
exercises.explanation: Each category group is summarized by adding its product stock quantities.

exercises.title: Average consultant rate by specialty
exercises.instructions: Display each specialty and its average consultant hourly rate.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT specialty, AVG(hourly_rate) AS average_rate FROM consultants GROUP BY specialty;
hints: Group by the category that defines each specialty.
exercises.explanation: AVG calculates a separate mean hourly rate for each specialty.

exercises.title: Total sales quantity by product
exercises.instructions: Display each product ID and the total quantity sold across all order lines.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS quantity_sold FROM order_items GROUP BY product_id;
hints: Group line items by product ID and sum quantity.
exercises.explanation: SUM adds the quantities for each product across all order-item rows.

exercises.title: Project count by client and status
exercises.instructions: Show each client ID and project status combination with its project count.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT client_id, project_status, COUNT(*) AS project_count FROM projects GROUP BY client_id, project_status;
hints: Group by both attributes to create one group per combination.
exercises.explanation: The two grouping columns form distinct client-status groups, and COUNT returns the number of projects in each group.

exercises.title: Task hours by employee and project
exercises.instructions: Display employee ID, project name and total task hours for each employee-project combination.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT employee_id, project_name, SUM(hours) AS total_hours FROM tasks GROUP BY employee_id, project_name;
hints: Use both employee and project name in GROUP BY.
exercises.explanation: The grouping forms one result per employee-project pair, and SUM adds its task hours.

exercises.title: Participant counts by training session
exercises.instructions: Show each session ID and the number of participants registered for it.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT session_id, COUNT(*) AS participant_count FROM participants GROUP BY session_id;
hints: Group participants by their session ID.
exercises.explanation: Each session ID forms a group; participants with a missing session ID form a NULL group.

exercises.title: Average order value by shipping city
exercises.instructions: Display each shipping city and the average order-line value for orders shipped to that city.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT o.shipping_city, AVG(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS average_line_value FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id GROUP BY o.shipping_city;
hints: Join orders to their lines, then group by shipping city.
exercises.explanation: The join associates each line with its shipping city; AVG calculates the mean line value within each city.

exercises.title: Department salary range
exercises.instructions: Show department IDs with the minimum and maximum salary in each department.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT department_id, MIN(salary) AS lowest_salary, MAX(salary) AS highest_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;
hints: Use MIN and MAX after grouping by department.
exercises.explanation: The aggregates calculate salary bounds for each department group.

exercises.title: Course enrollment totals and grades
exercises.instructions: Display course ID, enrollment count and average grade for each course.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS enrollment_count, AVG(final_grade) AS average_grade FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;
hints: Two aggregate functions can summarize the same group.
exercises.explanation: COUNT(*) includes every enrollment while AVG ignores rows whose final_grade is NULL.

exercises.title: Project budgets by client city
exercises.instructions: Display the client city and total project budget for each city.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.city, SUM(p.budget) AS total_budget FROM clients c JOIN projects p ON c.client_id = p.client_id GROUP BY c.city;
hints: Join projects to clients before grouping by city.
exercises.explanation: The join supplies the city for each project; SUM adds budgets within each city group.

exercises.title: Order quantities by product and order
exercises.instructions: Display order ID, product ID and the total quantity for each order-product combination.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT order_id, product_id, SUM(quantity) AS total_quantity FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id, product_id;
hints: Group using both key columns.
exercises.explanation: Each order-product pair is a group, and SUM totals the quantity recorded for that pair.

exercises.title: Average project assignment hours by consultant and role
exercises.instructions: Show consultant ID, role name and average hours worked for each consultant-role combination.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT consultant_id, role_name, AVG(hours_worked) AS average_hours FROM project_assignments GROUP BY consultant_id, role_name;
hints: Group by both consultant and role.
exercises.explanation: The grouping separates each role per consultant and AVG calculates the mean recorded hours in that group.

exercises.title: Training duration by trainer and date year
exercises.instructions: Display trainer ID and the year of the session date with the total duration of sessions in each combination.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT trainer_id, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM session_date) AS session_year, SUM(duration_hours) AS total_duration FROM training_sessions GROUP BY trainer_id, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM session_date);
hints: The selected date expression must also appear in GROUP BY.
exercises.explanation: The grouping combines trainer and session year; SUM totals the session duration for each group.

exercises.title: Total sales value by customer
exercises.instructions: Display customer ID and their total order value using order lines joined through orders.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS customer_total FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id GROUP BY o.customer_id;
hints: Join line values to orders, then group by customer.
exercises.explanation: The join associates each order line with a customer; the SUM calculates each customer’s combined line value.

exercises.title: Departments with many employees
exercises.instructions: Show department IDs with more than three employees.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS employee_count FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;
hints: HAVING filters groups based on an aggregate.
exercises.explanation: The grouping creates department groups and HAVING keeps only groups with more than three employees.

exercises.title: Product categories with a large catalogue
exercises.instructions: Display category IDs whose product count is at least three.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT category_id, COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
hints: Use HAVING after grouping to test the group count.
exercises.explanation: HAVING evaluates the number of products in each category group.

exercises.title: Courses with a high average grade
exercises.instructions: Show course IDs whose average recorded final grade is at least 85.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT course_id, AVG(final_grade) AS average_grade FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING AVG(final_grade) >= 85;
hints: Filter groups using the AVG result.
exercises.explanation: HAVING keeps only course groups whose known grades average 85 or higher.

exercises.title: Consultant specialties with average rate above 110
exercises.instructions: Display specialties whose average hourly rate is greater than 110.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT specialty, AVG(hourly_rate) AS average_rate FROM consultants GROUP BY specialty HAVING AVG(hourly_rate) > 110;
hints: The aggregate condition belongs in HAVING.
exercises.explanation: HAVING filters the specialty groups after AVG has calculated each group’s mean rate.

exercises.title: Filter orders before counting by status
exercises.instructions: For orders placed from April through July 2025, display each status and its order count.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT order_status, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2025-04-01' AND '2025-07-31' GROUP BY order_status;
hints: Use WHERE for the date restriction before grouping.
exercises.explanation: WHERE removes out-of-range order rows first; GROUP BY then counts the remaining orders per status.

exercises.title: Task hours per employee for named projects
exercises.instructions: For tasks on Atlas or Beacon, show employee IDs with total recorded hours above 15.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT employee_id, SUM(hours) AS total_hours FROM tasks WHERE project_name IN ('Atlas', 'Beacon') GROUP BY employee_id HAVING SUM(hours) > 15;
hints: Filter task rows in WHERE, then filter employee groups in HAVING.
exercises.explanation: WHERE limits the tasks to two projects; HAVING keeps employees whose summed hours exceed 15.

exercises.title: Projects with multiple assignments
exercises.instructions: Display project IDs with at least two assignment records.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT project_id, COUNT(*) AS assignment_count FROM project_assignments GROUP BY project_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
hints: Count assignments by project and filter the groups.
exercises.explanation: HAVING keeps projects whose assignment group contains two or more rows.

exercises.title: Revenue by product after quantity filter
exercises.instructions: For order lines with quantity at least two, show product IDs and total line value for products whose total exceeds 100.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS product_revenue FROM order_items WHERE quantity >= 2 GROUP BY product_id HAVING SUM(quantity * unit_price) > 100;
hints: WHERE filters individual lines; HAVING filters the product totals.
exercises.explanation: The query removes small-quantity lines first, then totals qualifying line values by product and keeps totals above 100.

exercises.title: Course averages for students with recorded grades
exercises.instructions: For enrollments with a recorded grade, display course IDs and average grades for course groups with at least two graded records.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT course_id, AVG(final_grade) AS average_grade FROM enrollments WHERE final_grade IS NOT NULL GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(final_grade) >= 2;
hints: Filter out NULL grades first, then count known grades within each course.
exercises.explanation: WHERE ensures only known grades enter the groups; HAVING requires at least two such records per course.

exercises.title: Consultants with substantial recorded project hours
exercises.instructions: For assignments with at least 80 recorded hours, display consultant IDs and total hours for consultants whose total exceeds 150.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT consultant_id, SUM(hours_worked) AS total_hours FROM project_assignments WHERE hours_worked >= 80 GROUP BY consultant_id HAVING SUM(hours_worked) > 150;
hints: Use WHERE for the per-assignment threshold and HAVING for the consultant total.
exercises.explanation: The query filters assignment rows first and then keeps consultant groups with more than 150 qualifying hours.

exercises.title: Cities with sufficient customer records
exercises.instructions: Display cities with more than one customer, considering only customers whose credit limit is known.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customer_count FROM customers WHERE credit_limit IS NOT NULL GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
hints: WHERE removes missing credit limits before the city groups are counted.
exercises.explanation: Only customers with a recorded credit limit enter the groups; HAVING retains cities with multiple qualifying customers.

exercises.title: Projects by client with active work only
exercises.instructions: For active projects, display each client ID and total active budget where the combined budget is above 200000.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT client_id, SUM(budget) AS active_budget FROM projects WHERE project_status = 'active' GROUP BY client_id HAVING SUM(budget) > 200000;
hints: Apply the status condition before grouping and the sum threshold after grouping.
exercises.explanation: WHERE limits the source rows to active projects; HAVING filters client totals after summing their budgets.

exercises.title: Teachers with multiple assigned sections
exercises.instructions: Display teacher IDs with more than one section assigned.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT teacher_id, COUNT(*) AS section_count FROM class_sections GROUP BY teacher_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
hints: Group sections by teacher, then apply a count condition.
exercises.explanation: HAVING checks each teacher’s section count and excludes groups with one or fewer sections.

exercises.title: Departments with high average salaries after row filter
exercises.instructions: For employees earning more than 50000, display department IDs whose average salary is above 65000.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS average_salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000 GROUP BY department_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 65000;
hints: Use WHERE for the individual salary minimum and HAVING for the department average.
exercises.explanation: Only qualifying employees are grouped; HAVING then tests the average in each department.

exercises.title: Sessions with high assessment averages
exercises.instructions: For participants with recorded assessment scores, show session IDs whose average score is at least 85.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT session_id, AVG(assessment_score) AS average_score FROM participants WHERE assessment_score IS NOT NULL GROUP BY session_id HAVING AVG(assessment_score) >= 85;
hints: Exclude missing scores before calculating each session’s average.
exercises.explanation: WHERE removes NULL assessments; HAVING keeps session groups with an average of at least 85.

exercises.title: All departments and any employees
exercises.instructions: Display every department name together with employee names where employees are assigned. Keep departments even when no employee matches.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT d.department_name, e.first_name, e.last_name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.department_id = e.department_id;
hints: Place departments on the left side of LEFT JOIN.
exercises.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves every department; department rows without employees have NULL employee columns.

exercises.title: All customers and their orders
exercises.instructions: Display every customer name and any matching order ID, including customers who have never placed an order.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, o.order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
hints: Keep customers in the left table.
exercises.explanation: LEFT JOIN returns all customers and fills order columns with NULL where there is no order.

exercises.title: All courses and enrolled student IDs
exercises.instructions: Display every course title and matching student IDs for courses with enrollments, retaining courses without any enrollment.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.course_title, e.student_id FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id;
hints: Use courses as the left table so empty courses remain.
exercises.explanation: The LEFT JOIN preserves all courses and supplies NULL for student IDs when no enrollment exists.

exercises.title: All projects and staffing records
exercises.instructions: Show every project name with any assigned consultant ID, including projects without assignments.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.project_name, a.consultant_id FROM projects p LEFT JOIN project_assignments a ON p.project_id = a.project_id;
hints: Start from projects and preserve the left-side records.
exercises.explanation: Projects remain in the result even if no project_assignments row matches.

exercises.title: Find customers without orders
exercises.instructions: Return customer IDs and names for customers who have no matching order.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
hints: After the LEFT JOIN, test the right table’s primary key for NULL.
exercises.explanation: A missing order_id identifies customers for whom the join found no matching order.

exercises.title: Find courses without enrollments
exercises.instructions: Display course IDs and titles for courses with no enrollment records.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.course_id, c.course_title FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id WHERE e.student_id IS NULL;
hints: Keep all courses, then retain rows with no right-side key match.
exercises.explanation: The enrollment student_id is non-NULL in every real enrollment, so NULL identifies an unmatched course row.

exercises.title: Find employees without tasks
exercises.instructions: Display employee names for employees who have no matching task record.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN tasks t ON e.employee_id = t.employee_id WHERE t.task_id IS NULL;
hints: Use LEFT JOIN and check the task primary key.
exercises.explanation: A NULL task_id indicates that the employee has no matching task row.

exercises.title: Find projects without assigned consultants
exercises.instructions: Return project IDs and names where no assignment row exists.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.project_id, p.project_name FROM projects p LEFT JOIN project_assignments a ON p.project_id = a.project_id WHERE a.consultant_id IS NULL;
hints: Test a non-NULL join-key column from the right table.
exercises.explanation: The consultant_id is required in a real assignment; NULL therefore identifies projects with no assignment.

exercises.title: Preserve every location
exercises.instructions: Display all locations and any departments assigned to them, keeping locations that currently have no department.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT l.city, d.department_name FROM departments d RIGHT JOIN locations l ON d.location_id = l.location_id;
hints: RIGHT JOIN preserves the rows from the table written on the right.
exercises.explanation: The right join keeps every location and returns NULL department columns for unused locations.

exercises.title: Preserve every category
exercises.instructions: Display all product categories and any matching products, retaining categories with no products.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.product_name, c.category_name FROM products p RIGHT JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id;
hints: Categories must be the right-hand table to preserve all of them.
exercises.explanation: RIGHT JOIN keeps every category and returns NULL product details when no product matches.

exercises.title: All departments and employee department references
exercises.instructions: Display department names and employee names, retaining unmatched rows from both tables.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT d.department_name, e.first_name, e.last_name FROM departments d FULL JOIN employees e ON d.department_id = e.department_id;
hints: FULL JOIN retains matched rows plus unmatched rows from both sides.
exercises.explanation: Departments without employees and employees without a matching department are both preserved; absent-side columns are NULL.

exercises.title: All clients and project client references
exercises.instructions: Display client names and project names, including clients without projects and any project rows with no matching client.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.client_name, p.project_name FROM clients c FULL JOIN projects p ON c.client_id = p.client_id;
hints: Use FULL JOIN to retain all rows from both tables.
exercises.explanation: The full join preserves unmatched clients and unmatched projects as well as matched pairs.

exercises.title: Count tasks for every employee
exercises.instructions: Display every employee ID and the number of matching tasks, including employees with no tasks.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.employee_id, COUNT(t.task_id) AS task_count FROM employees e LEFT JOIN tasks t ON e.employee_id = t.employee_id GROUP BY e.employee_id;
hints: After a LEFT JOIN, count a non-NULL right-table key rather than COUNT(*).
exercises.explanation: COUNT(t.task_id) counts only real matching task rows; COUNT(*) would count the preserved employee row even when no task matched.

exercises.title: Count orders for every customer
exercises.instructions: Display every customer ID and their number of matching orders, including customers with zero orders.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id;
hints: Use the customer table as the preserved side and count the order key.
exercises.explanation: The LEFT JOIN retains customers with no orders; COUNT(o.order_id) returns zero for their unmatched row.

exercises.title: Count students per course including empty courses
exercises.instructions: Display each course ID and the number of matching enrollment records, including courses with no enrollment.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.course_id, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrollment_count FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id GROUP BY c.course_id;
hints: Keep courses and count the non-NULL enrollment key.
exercises.explanation: Every course remains in the result; COUNT(e.student_id) counts only actual enrollment matches.

exercises.title: Count consultants per project including unstaffed work
exercises.instructions: Display every project ID and the number of consultant assignments, including projects with none.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.project_id, COUNT(a.consultant_id) AS consultant_count FROM projects p LEFT JOIN project_assignments a ON p.project_id = a.project_id GROUP BY p.project_id;
hints: Count the right-side assignment key after a LEFT JOIN.
exercises.explanation: COUNT(a.consultant_id) returns zero for a project without an assignment because the right-side key is NULL.

exercises.title: All right-side sessions and participants
exercises.instructions: Display every training session and any participant names, retaining sessions without participants. Put training_sessions on the right side of the join.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT s.session_title, p.participant_name FROM participants p RIGHT JOIN training_sessions s ON p.session_id = s.session_id;
hints: RIGHT JOIN keeps all rows from training_sessions in this query.
exercises.explanation: The right join preserves every session and supplies NULL participant names for sessions without registrations.

exercises.title: All employees and all department records
exercises.instructions: Return employee IDs and department IDs so that employees with NULL or unmatched departments and departments with no employees are both represented.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT e.employee_id, e.department_id AS employee_department_id, d.department_id AS listed_department_id, d.department_name FROM employees e FULL JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
hints: Use FULL JOIN and display identifiers from both sides to distinguish unmatched rows.
exercises.explanation: The full join preserves every employee and every department, showing NULL columns for whichever side has no match.

exercises.title: Total quantity sold by category
exercises.instructions: Display each product category and the total units sold for that category.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.category_name, SUM(oi.quantity) AS units_sold FROM categories c JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id GROUP BY c.category_name;
hints: Join categories to products and order lines before grouping.
exercises.explanation: The joins connect each sold product to its category; GROUP BY creates category groups and SUM totals their quantities.

exercises.title: Average assignment hours by client
exercises.instructions: Display client names and the average project assignment hours associated with each client.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT cl.client_name, AVG(a.hours_worked) AS average_assignment_hours FROM clients cl JOIN projects p ON cl.client_id = p.client_id JOIN project_assignments a ON p.project_id = a.project_id GROUP BY cl.client_name;
hints: Join clients to projects and assignments, then group by client name.
exercises.explanation: The joins attribute each assignment to a client; AVG calculates each client’s mean recorded assignment hours.

exercises.title: Departments with at least one employee
exercises.instructions: Display all departments that have at least one employee and show the number of employees in each.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT d.department_name, COUNT(e.employee_id) AS employee_count FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.department_id = e.department_id GROUP BY d.department_id, d.department_name HAVING COUNT(e.employee_id) >= 1;
hints: Keep departments with LEFT JOIN, group by department and filter the matched employee count.
exercises.explanation: The LEFT JOIN preserves departments; COUNT(e.employee_id) counts only actual matches and HAVING removes departments with zero employees.

exercises.title: Customers with two or more orders
exercises.instructions: Display customer names and their order counts for customers with at least two orders.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) >= 2;
hints: Use a LEFT JOIN, group by the customer details and filter the count.
exercises.explanation: COUNT(o.order_id) measures actual orders, and HAVING retains customers with at least two matching orders.

exercises.title: Average grade by teacher
exercises.instructions: Display teacher names and the average final grade of enrollments in sections taught by each teacher.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT t.teacher_id, t.first_name, t.last_name, AVG(e.final_grade) AS average_grade FROM teachers t JOIN class_sections s ON t.teacher_id = s.teacher_id JOIN enrollments e ON s.section_id = e.section_id AND s.course_id = e.course_id GROUP BY t.teacher_id, t.first_name, t.last_name;
hints: Join teachers to sections and enrollments using both section key columns, then group by teacher.
exercises.explanation: The joins connect grades to the teacher responsible for the section; AVG calculates each teacher’s mean recorded grade.

exercises.title: Show products that have never been ordered
exercises.instructions: Display product IDs and names for products that do not appear in any order line.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name FROM products p LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id WHERE oi.order_id IS NULL;
hints: Use a LEFT JOIN and test the right-side primary-key component.
exercises.explanation: An order_id is always present for a real order line, so NULL identifies products with no matching order item.

exercises.title: Total spending by customer above threshold
exercises.instructions: Display customer IDs and total order value for customers whose combined order-line value exceeds 1000.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS customer_spending FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id GROUP BY o.customer_id HAVING SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) > 1000;
hints: Join orders to their lines, group by customer and filter with HAVING.
exercises.explanation: SUM calculates the value of the customer’s line items; HAVING keeps customers whose total exceeds 1000.

exercises.title: Count participants for every session with capacity
exercises.instructions: Display every session title, its maximum capacity and its number of registered participants, including sessions with none.
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.referenceSolution: SELECT s.session_title, s.max_participants, COUNT(p.participant_id) AS registered_count FROM training_sessions s LEFT JOIN participants p ON s.session_id = p.session_id GROUP BY s.session_id, s.session_title, s.max_participants;
hints: Preserve every session, count the participant primary key and group by the selected session details.
exercises.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps empty sessions; COUNT(participant_id) returns zero for unmatched sessions while the capacity remains available.

exercises.title: COUNT star compared with COUNT column
exercises.instructions: Which statement about COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) is correct?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values
COUNT(column) counts all rows including NULL
exercises.explanation: COUNT(*) counts every row, while COUNT(column) ignores rows where that column is NULL.

exercises.title: Purpose of GROUP BY
exercises.instructions: What does GROUP BY do in an aggregate query?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: Creates groups so aggregates are calculated per group
exercises.explanation: GROUP BY forms one group for each distinct combination of the grouping columns.

exercises.title: WHERE or HAVING
exercises.instructions: Which clause should filter groups based on AVG(salary)?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.explanation: HAVING filters groups after aggregate values have been calculated.

exercises.title: LEFT JOIN row preservation
exercises.instructions: Which table’s rows are all preserved by a LEFT JOIN?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves every row from the left table and fills unmatched right-side columns with NULL.

exercises.title: FULL JOIN behavior
exercises.instructions: What does FULL JOIN return?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: All left rows but no right-only rows
All right rows but no left-only rows
Matching rows plus unmatched rows from both sides
exercises.explanation: FULL JOIN retains all rows from both tables, with NULLs for values on the side without a match.

exercises.title: How AVG treats NULL
exercises.instructions: How does AVG(column) handle NULL values?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: Returns NULL if any row is NULL
exercises.explanation: Most aggregate functions, including AVG, ignore NULL values.

exercises.title: Correct location for row filters
exercises.instructions: A condition such as salary > 50000 uses a plain column and should normally appear in which clause before grouping?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING is for conditions on groups.

exercises.title: Identify unmatched right-side rows
exercises.instructions: After a LEFT JOIN, which test is commonly used to find left-side rows with no match?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
exercises.explanation: A non-NULL key from the right table is NULL in an unmatched outer-join row.

exercises.title: SELECT columns with GROUP BY
exercises.instructions: In a grouped query, what must be true of a plain column in SELECT that is not inside an aggregate?
exercises.provenance: sql-cheat-sheet.md; sql.md (course scope and exercise specification)
options: It must be in ORDER BY only
It must be listed in GROUP BY
It must be a foreign key
exercises.explanation: Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must be included in GROUP BY.
